explanation: It has more than double the production of the runner-up state, South Dakota. Haha, suck it, SoDak!

question: The only government-owned general services bank (meaning, it is a bank that the general public can use) in the US is found in this state.
explanation: The Bank of North Dakota was founded in 1909 and has been profitable every year since, and those profits either fund development projects or go into the state's general fund.

question: This state has a Pharmacy Ownership Law that means pharmacies must be at least 51% owned by pharmacists, meaning the big chains do not operate there.
explanation: The state does have some CVS stores that were in existence before the law passed in 1963. It also has one Walgreens that cannot dispense prescription meds.

question: The world's largest scrap metal sculpture (Geese in Flight) was made by Gary Greff in 2001 in this state, on a road running between Regent and Gladstone south of I-94.
explanation: At 110 ft (33m) tall and 154 ft (47m) wide, it is part of a series of 8 sculptures on the 32 mile (51 km) long "Enchanted Highway".

question: A city (at one point nicknamed 'the mistake on the lake') in this state was the first to be lit by electric lights, in 1879.
explanation: Cleveland had 12 lights installed around the Public Square as a test of the newly developed electric lights.

question: The first traffic light in the US was installed in 1914 in this state
explanation: The first person to run a red light occurred 6 minutes after this light was installed.

question: The first professional, paid baseball team, the Red Stockings, was established in 1869 in this state, and eventually became the Atlanta Braves.
explanation: The Red Socks were a founding member of the National League in 1876 in Cincinnati, but played one season there before moving to Boston for 83 years, then Milwaukee for 12 years, and finally Atlanta since 1966.

question: The Rock and Roll Hall of Fame can be found in this state
explanation: The museum was designed by I.M. Pei and was sited in Cleveland in part because local DJ Alan Freed coined the term 'rock and roll' in the 1950s. It had nothing to do with the city's pledge of $65 million in public money to fund construction.

question: The Pro Football Hall of Fame is located in Canton in this state
explanation: Canton was where what would become the NFL was founded in 1920.

question: The first man to walk on the moon (in July 1969), Neil Armstrong, hailed from Wapakoneta in this state.
explanation: In 1985, he was part of a group including Edmund Hillary, Steve Fossett and Patrick Morrow that went to the North Pole.

question: This state's flag is the only one that is not a rectangular design, and is known as a "burgee"
explanation: It is a triangular swallowtail flag, and has an official 17-step folding process, symbolizing that it was the 17th state in the Union.

question: The first co-educational college, Oberlin, in the US is in this state
explanation: The town of Oberlin is also where the Anti-Saloon League was founded in 1893, which was a major force behind Prohibition.

question: Thomas Edison was born in Milan in this state in 1847, but grew up in Michigan
explanation: Edison had 1,093 US patents in his name, and 2,332 patents worldwide.

question: The Olympic gold medalist Jesse Owens was born in Alabama but grew up in this state when his family moved north for better opportunities.
explanation: At a 1935 track meet in Ann Arbor, MI, he broke 3 world records and tied a fourth, all in less than an hour, in a feat known as the "greatest 45 minutes ever in sport."

question: This state is known as the Buckeye state, named after a common tree in the area
explanation: Buckeye candy is made from peanut butter fudge partially dipped in chocolate and is made to look like a buckeye seed.

question: Which state's first permanent settlement was named Marietta, after Marie Antoinette?
explanation: She ordered that France help the US in its battle for independence from Britain.

question: The world's first parking meter was installed in this state in July 1935.
explanation: The first contested parking ticket was issued a month later to Rev. C.H. North, a preacher claiming he went into a store to get change for the meter. A judge dismissed the ticket, possibly the last time that excuse worked.

question: The National Cowboy Hall of Fame is located in this state
explanation: The museum has the world's most extensive collection of rodeo photographs as well as one of the largest barbed wire collections.

question: The first shopping cart was introduced at the Humpty Dumpty store in this state in 1937
explanation: It took a while for customers to accept Sylvan Goldman's invention, as women thought it was too much like pushing a baby carriage.

question: The only state with an official state meal is _____, and includes chicken fried steak, barbecue pork, sausage and gravy.
explanation: It also includes fried okra, squash, cornbread, grits, corn, black-eyed peas, strawberries, and pecan pie. The ensuing cardiac event is just a bonus.

question: This state's state vegetable is actually the watermelon, a fruit, because the spot of state fruit was already claimed by the strawberry.
explanation: A watermelon is a type of berry called a pepo, meaning it produces a large amount of seeds and has a tough outer skin.

question: This state is where Garth Brooks, the artist with the most diamond-status (10 million or more copies) records, grew up.
explanation: Garth Brooks has more diamond certified albums (9) than any other performer, including the Beatles and Led Zeppelin. He has lived in TN since 1990, but was born and grew up in OK.

question: This is the only state capital with an oil well underneath it, even though it ran dry in 1986.
explanation: The well, known as Petunia #1 because it was drilled through a flower bed, produced over 1.5 million barrels of oil during its life.

question: This state produces the most hazelnuts of any state in the US
explanation: Also known as filberts, Turkey produces about 70% of the world's hazelnuts. Oregon produces 99% of the US crop.

question: The Lewis and Clark expedition officially reached the Pacific Ocean in this state in 1805.
explanation: Astoria is the oldest city in Oregon and the first American settlement west of the Rockies. It is also where Goonies was filmed.

question: This is the only state with a flag that has a different design on each side, with one side having the state mammal.
explanation: The front side has the state seal, and the reverse has a beaver.

question: The deepest lake in the US is found in this state
explanation: Crater Lake has no inlet or outlet rivers, is 1,949 ft (594m) deep, and 9th deepest in the world.

question: The deepest river gorge in the US is found on the border of Idaho and this state.
explanation: Hell's Canyon is 7,993 ft (2,436m) deep (1,800 ft deeper than the Grand Canyon) and is carved by the Snake River.

question: The largest sea cave in the US is found in this state
explanation: At 1,315 ft (400m), it is the longest sea cave in the US and is the only known mainland rookery for the Steller's sea lion.

question: The largest clear-span wooden structure in the world housed blimps during WWII in this state
explanation: At 1,072 ft (327m) long, 296 ft (90m) wide and 192 ft (59m) tall, hangar B of Naval Air Station Tillamook was built to house blimps during WWII.

question: In which state would you find Powell's City of Books, the largest independent bookstore in the world?
explanation: Founded in 1971 by Michael Powell, the City of Books flagship store has 68,000 sq ft and 3,500 different sections.

question: One of the state universities of this state uses orange as one of its colors (the other being black) in honor of the tooth color of its mascot (which is also the state mammal).
explanation: Beavers are the second largest rodent and they have orange teeth due to iron-rich enamel.

question: The nation's first commercial oil well was in this state in 1859
explanation: The Drake Well outside Titusville was 69 ft (21m) deep and was the first that was drilled specifically to obtain oil.

question: This state has 2 of the original teams that formed what became Major League Baseball.
explanation: The Pittsburgh Pirates were formed in 1882 and the Philadelphia Phillies started in 1883.

question: The chocolate capital of the US is in Hershey, in this state
explanation: Milton Hershey also founded a private school for 'impoverished children' and it has a $17 billion endowment, making it the wealthiest private K-12 school in the US.

question: This state has what is considered to be the oldest residential street in the country
explanation: Elfreth's Alley in Philadelphia was created in 1702 and still has 32 houses.

question: The first computer was invented in this state (but not the first to be widely sold, that was the Altair 8800 from New Mexico)
explanation: The Electronic Numerical Integrator and Computer (ENIAC) was built by Mauchly and Eckert at the University of Pennsylvania and was dedicated in 1946. It filled a 20 by 40 foot room and weighed 30 tons!

question: This state is home of the annual Punxsutawney Phil Groundhog Day festivities.
explanation: The first official trek to Gobbler's Knob occurred on Feb 2, 1887. Phil has never seen his shadow.

question: There are three locations in this state where you can stand in one spot and see 3 states at once.
explanation: They are in the extreme southwest (where you can see Ohio, West Virginia and PA); in the extreme northeast (where you can see New York, New Jersey and PA); and near the 'tri-state marker' (where you can see Delaware, Maryland and PA).

question: The Liberty Bell is one of the main tourist attractions in this state
explanation: Cast in 1752, it first cracked when it was rung after arriving in the city, and again 73 years later when rung to commemorate George Washington's birthday. Despite multiple theories, the actual reason for the crack is unknown.

question: The first hospital in the US was founded in this state, and was co-founded by Benjamin Franklin in 1751.
explanation: The hospital was founded to care for the poor and sick. The first patient was a woman with "Lunacy".

question: This state is home of the first KDKA commercial radio broadcasting station in the US, in 1920.
explanation: The station first broadcast from the Westinghouse plant in Pittsburgh. Most stations at that time were amateur.

question: The first World Series was played in 1903 between Boston and a city in this state.
explanation: Boston beat the Pittsburgh Pirates, 5 games to 3, with Boston winning the last 4 games in a row. Tickets cost 50 cents.

question: The oldest public zoo in the US is located in this state
explanation: The Philadelphia Zoo opened on July 1, 1874, and now has 1,300 animals and receives 1.2 million visitors each year.

question: This state has over 120 covered bridges, second most in the US after Pennsylvania. (Not a trivia question)
explanation: Ohio has the second most with a little over 120 covered bridges still standing. Pennsy has over 200.

question: This state's name is derived from a Dutch island that means "red island".
explanation: Italian explorer Giovanni da Verrazzano thought the island looked similar to one off the coast of Italy. Also, "Rhode" is pronounced "Rod".

question: This state's official beverage is coffee milk, because a large number of the state's residents are originally from Portugal, which is a major coffee producer.
explanation: It is made by mixing coffee extract with milk and it has been sold in the state since the 1930s.

question: The first circus in the US was held in this state in 1774.
explanation: It was put on by a Brit named John Bill Ricketts and consisted of a horse riding show, some rope tricks and a clown. It was considered a pretty good show for 1774, when not much happened anyway.

question: The tennis Hall of Fame can be found in this state.
explanation: Founded in 1954, it is where the first US National Championship was held in 1881, where 33 men competed. The first women's event was held in 1887.

question: The first Quonset huts, light weight pre-fab structures used during WWII, were made in this state.
explanation: They were first used by the US Navy and could be assembled by 4-6 men in 1-2 days, and were a version of the British Nissen huts.

question: Newport in this state is known as the "Sailing Capital of the World".
explanation: With the nickname, it should come as no surprise that the state also boasts a large number of beautiful beaches.

question: This is the smallest US state in area, as well as being the state with the longest official name.
explanation: The State of Rhode Island and Providence Plantations is its actual name. Just try to get that on a license plate!

question: This state has no counties. They were abolished in 1961.
explanation: The state is divided into 39 cities and towns that handle things that are typically run by a county, such as law enforcement, schools, and trash collection.

question: What state's official nickname is the Palmetto State?
explanation: The palmetto is known for its spongy wood, which absorbed cannonballs during the Revolutionary War. The tree is on the state flag.

question: This state has the only tea plantation in the US.
explanation: Charleston Tea Garden is on Wadmalaw Island and has been producing tea since 1987, and you can tour it.

question: Hootie and the Blowfish met and started as a band at the University of this state in 1986.
explanation: The band's name comes from the nicknames of two college friends. The frontman, Darius Rucker, has had a successful career as a country artist.

question: This state has a town called Ninety Six, so named for a misunderstanding of how many miles it was to the closest Native American village.
explanation: The town was established in the 1700s as a trading post and was the site of a Revolutionary War battle.

question: This state is known for its sweet peaches
explanation: While Georgia is known as the Peach State, S. Carolina actually produces more of them, with about 17,600 tons in 2020. So, haha Georgia, suck it!

question: What is the only state to share its name with a city in the Netherlands?
explanation: South Caralina is named after Charles I of England but this is not correct! Should not have been added.

question: This state has 187 miles of coastline, the 8th fewest of all the coastal states.
explanation: Florida has 1350 miles of coastline. Even Ohio has more than South Carolina! And Ohio doesn't even have a coastline!

question: The first state capital, in this state, was destroyed in 1865.
explanation: Columbia was burned to the ground by General Sherman's troops and little was left standing.

question: The Crazy Horse Memorial, a sculpture of a Lakota warrior on horseback, is carved out of the Black Hills of this state.
explanation: When completed, it will be the world's largest mountain carving, at 641 ft (195m) long and 563 ft (172m) high.

question: Which state contains Wall Drug, the tourist stop famous for advertising signs along hundreds of miles of Interstate?
explanation: A pharmacist named Ted Hustead bought the drugstore in Wall, SD in 1931 and was nearly bankrupt before his wife suggested giving away free ice water to parched travelers. That, and all the signs, turned it into a tourist mecca.

question: The Homestake gold mine, the largest and deepest in North America, used to be located in this state.
explanation: It closed in 2002 after 126 years of operation and now hosts the Sanford Underground Research Facility, where scientists are studying dark matter.

question: This state's official dessert is kuchen, a cake made with German sweet dough and various fruit fillings.
explanation: Due to a large influx of German immigrants in the 1880s, the dessert became very popular in the state.

question: What is the only state whose borders are entirely lines of latitude and longitude?
explanation: You were so close but so far. You fell into the classic trap!

question: Which state has the official motto "Under God the People Rule?"
explanation: Despite being a theocracy, it does not have a state religion. At least they are up front about it.

question: The first archeological discovery of a tyrannosaurus rex, "Sue", was found in this state in 1990
explanation: It is the most complete T-Rex fossil ever discovered, at 90% complete, and measures over 40 ft long and 13 ft high.

question: The first inhabitants of the South were referred to as Tennesseans, and Tennessee derives its name from the old Yuchi Indian word, 'Tana-see,' meaning ______. (State trivia question)
explanation: After Tennessee was admitted to the union in 1796, settlers began calling themselves 'Tennesseans'.

question: The biggest earthquake in this state's history, the 1811-1812 New Madrid earthquakes, caused the Mississippi River to flow backwards for two days (State trivia question).
explanation: The 1811-1812 New Madrid earthquakes were the largest to ever occur on the North American continent east of the Rocky Mountains.

question: This state is home to the world's only museum dedicated to pinball (State trivia question)
explanation: Located in Knoxville, The Pinball Museum features nearly 100 machines, many of which are available to play. All proceeds go to charity.

question: One of the most visited and picturesque areas in the country can be found in the eastern section of this state (State trivia question).
explanation: Home to the Great Smoky Mountains National Park, which spans over 520,000 acres, it draws approximately 14 million visitors every year.

question: Which state's official state song has been changed 9 times due to complaints of racist lyrics? (State trivia question)
explanation: It has had 9 official state songs (currently it has 8), beginning with 'My Homeland Tennessee', adopted in 1925. All other songs were added between 1935 and 1965.

question: This state has 3 cities that boast their own style of BBQ, each wildly different from each other.(State trivia question)
explanation: Memphis BBQ uses a dry rub with ribs and pork, West Tennessee BBQ uses a wet mop sauce for pulled pork, and Eastern Tennessee BBQ is known for its tomato-based BBQ with pork shoulder.

question: One of the most well known music cities in the world is found in this state.(State trivia question)
explanation: Nashville is nicknamed Music City, and is considered the home of country music. Also home to the Grand Ol Opry!

question: This state has a city known as the "buckle on the Bible Belt"? (State trivia question)
explanation: Murfreesboro in is about 30 miles southeast of Nashville, and is the geographic center of the state. It has a large population of devout Christians and a multitude of churches.

question: This state boasts a road that traverses 10 of the 14 different climate zones in North America. (State trivia question)
explanation: Highway 170, also known as River Road, travels through 50 miles of the Big Bend region. Climate zones are characterized by average temperature ranges, rainfall, and latitude

question: This state's name derives from the Caddo Indian word teyshas, meaning friends, and is also known as the Friendship State (State trivia question)
explanation: The state is also known as the Lone Star State, owing to the single star on the state flag.

question: The Capitol building in this state is actually taller than the US Capitol building in Washington DC. (State trivia question)
explanation: The Texas capitol is 302.64 ft (92.24m) high while the US Capitol is 289 ft (88m) high. And the Washington Monument is still taller, in case you were wondering.

question: This state has 3 official "state somethings" that include a chile pepper.
explanation: New Mexico, which is also known as the Chile state. This question was added by accident.

question: This is the only state that was a sovereign nation before joining the US, after winning its independence from Mexico in 1836 (State trivia question)
explanation: After winning its independence from Mexico, Texas was known as the Republic of Texas for about 10 years before joining the US.

question: The original Dallas Cowboys were almost named the Steers, Rangers or Bluebonnets before settling on a name in this state. (State trivia question)
explanation: Since they are named after cowboys, the name seemed like a good fit, but it was the least favorite in a name-the-team contest held by the team.

question: This state, with over 860 native species of birds, has the highest number of native bird species of any other in the US. (State trivia question)
explanation: Most bird species migrate south to warmer climates in the winter, and for many migratory bird species, Texas is their winter home.

question: While the Alamo is a tourist stop that had a key role in the Texas Revolution, it was built by Spanish Catholics as a what? (State trivia question)
explanation: The Alamo was one of five missions that Spain established in what is now San Antonio. It started in 1718 and was a fort as well.

question: This state is where you can find the Great Salt Lake, the largest saltwater lake in the western hemisphere. (State trivia question)
explanation: The lake is about 75 miles (121 km) long by 35 miles (56 km) wide, and is too salty to swim in.

question: KFC Colonel Harland Sanders was never an actual Colonel, but the founder of another well known chain was a US Army colonel in this state.
explanation: Sanders got his colonel title from the governor of Kentucky. Harland Sanders - was Colonel Sanders not a real colonel?. Dave Thomas was a US Army colonel that was stationed in Utah.

question: The first McDonald's drive-thru was built in a city in this state, to make it easier for military personnel to grab a bite while in uniform. (State trivia question)
explanation: It was built in Sierra Vista near Fort Huachuca, an Army base.

question: The annual Sundance Film Festival is held in Park City in this state (State trivia question)
explanation: Named after the Robert Redford film Sundance Kid, the festival features hundreds of films and is a key stop for independent filmmakers to get their work shown. Some folks even use their real names.

question: This state has what is considered to be the world's largest copper mine, and is visible from space (State trivia question)
explanation: The Bingham Canyon Mine produces copper, gold, silver and molybdenum, and as of 2019, it was 0.75 miles (1.2 km) deep, 2.5 miles (4 km) wide and covered 1,900 acres (770 ha).

question: While its population is only about 3.3 million, this state has 5 national parks (Arches, Bryce Canyon, Canyonlands, Capitol Reef, Zion National Park).
explanation: California has the most with 9, while Alaska has 8. There are 63 total National Parks in the US.

question: This state is one of two that completely ban gambling in any form. The other is Hawaii, but which one is this?(State trivia question)
explanation: Hawaii does allow "social gambling", which it defines as bets between individuals, not in any business or public area, with no "house take".

question: In the 1890s, which state was the first one to give women the right to vote and later become the 44th state? (State Trivia question)
explanation: Wyoming actually was the first state to give women the right to vote, they just were'nt the 44th state to join the United States of America. This question should have been removed!

question: This is the least populated state on the East Coast, with just over 640,000 people (State trivia question)
explanation: The state is only about 40 miles from Canada. Its southern and western borders are only 1 hour from NYC by air.

question: The first state to outlaw slavery was the Republic of ___, before it joined the union. (State trivia question)
explanation: The republic was independent for 14 years and wrote into its constitution the outlawing of slavery.

question: This is the only state that banned billboards (in 1968). (State trivia question)
explanation: While the state has many ugly, run-down general stores that may detract from the scenery, at least they have no billboards to distract you!

question: This state has one of the few cities in the US that has never had a McDonald's. (State trivia question)
explanation: Since it is illegal to put up a billboard, the population is too small and spread out, and there are very few traffic lights, McDonalds has never bothered building in Stowe.

question: More than 1/2 of this state is covered in forest. (State trivia question)
explanation: While Maine is known as the Pine Tree State, 76% of it is covered with forest, compared to just over 50% for Vermont.

question: This state produces the most maple syrup of any in the US. (State trivia question)
explanation: While it produces 6% of the world's supply of maple syrup, that is small in comparison to Canada, which produces over 80%.

question: This state has almost the same number of dairy cows as people.(State trivia question)
explanation: While the number of cows has decreased slightly over the past few years, the state currently has about 125,000 cows, and 640,000 people.

question: The only US state that shares a land border with only one other state is ____.(State trivia question)
explanation: You really should pick the right answer.

question: While it is known for its peaches, peanuts and pecans, a different crop is actually this state's largest, netting more than $70 million in cash receipts in 2020.
explanation: The largest cash crop is actually soybeans (although they don't make for nearly as much of a nice pie).

question: Of the 50 US states, this one has the most cities that were originally named after British monarchs, such as Jamestown, Williamsburg and Portsmouth.
explanation: There are over 20 with names that can be traced back to the British royals. The name of the state itself comes from Queen Elizabeth I, also known as The Virgin Queen.

question: Arlington National Cemetery is located in this state, the largest military cemetery in the US
explanation: The cemetery is about 639 acres (259 hectares) and is the final resting place for over 400,000 veterans and their eligible dependents.

question: The Battle of Yorktown, the last significant battle of the Revolutionary War, was fought in this state.
explanation: It occurred in 1781 with the combined forces of America and France defeating the British, prompting the British government to begin negotiating an end to the war.

question: Mount Vernon, the home of George Washington, is located in this state.
explanation: He inherited the home in 1761 and greatly expanded the original structure. Washington is buried there in a family crypt.

question: This state is the birthplace of 8 US presidents.
explanation: Also known as the Mother of Presidents, those being George Washington, Thomas Jefferson, James Madison, James Monroe, William Henry Harrison, John Tyler, Zachary Taylor, and Woodrow Wilson.

question: Seattle in this state is where the World's Fair was held in 1962
explanation: More than 10 million people visited the fair, whose theme was "Space Age," and which featured the iconic Space Needle.

question: While much of the state is forested, this state grows more apples than any other in the US (although a distant second to China)
explanation: It produces about 70% of the apples grown in the US, at over 12 billion pounds per year. Also known for its delicious rainier cherries, too.

question: The lowest point in this state, where the Snake River enters the Columbia, is just 48 ft (15m)
explanation: This is also the lowest point in the Pacific Northwest region and about 14,400 ft (4,400m) lower than the highest point.

question: This is the only state to be named after a US president (although that president had never even been there!)
explanation: The state was named after George Washington, and he also never visited Washington, DC.

question: What is the only state that can be spelled using just one row on a QWERTY keyboard? (State trivia question)
explanation: It also has the fewest letters. The row is QWERTYUIOP.

question: The world’s first revolving restaurant, The Eye of the Needle, was built atop the Space Needle for the World Fair in Seattle in this state. (State trivia question)
explanation: The restaurant slowly rotates 360 degrees so guests can see all of Seattle while they enjoy their meal.

question: This state is only divided into 39 counties.(State trivia question)
explanation: Delaware has the fewest with just 3, while Texas has the most with 254.

question: This state is the only one that can claim to be part of two former countries.
explanation: Parts of the state were claimed by both Great Britain and Russia before it became part of the US. Now, can you show me where that is on the map?

question: West Virginia is the only state to secede from which side to join the Union?
explanation: West Virginia seceded from the confederacy and its request for statehood was granted in 1863, making it the only state to break off from another during the Civil War.

question: The New River, one of the oldest rivers in the world, goes through this state, flowing north against prevailing waterways and actually carving through the Appalachian Mountains.
explanation: The river is estimated to be between 360 million and 300 million years old and is only 320 miles long.

question: This state is the most obese in the US and, by an amazing coincidence, has the most fast food restaurants per capita. (State trivia question)
explanation: 41.2% of the population meets criteria for obesity, according to a 2023 study. The state has 49 fast food places per 100,000 residents.

question: The first brick paved street in the world, Summers Street, was laid in this state.
explanation: The street in Charleston was paved with bricks in 1870 and is still in use today.

question: Black bears can be found in all 55 counties in this state (State trivia question)
explanation: As of 2024, an estimated 12,000 black bears call the state home.

question: While some people live in the state, it is best known for its cheese, and is known as America's Dairyland (State trivia question)
explanation: Despite recent issues with farmers and water shortages in the west, the Dairy State has long been known for its dairy production. Go Packers!

question: The first ice cream sundae originated in this state (State trivia question)
explanation: It was created in 1881 by a druggist in Two Rivers, and was known as an ice cream soda without the soda syrup.

question: This state is the birthplace of the Republican Party, which was founded in 1854 (State trivia question)
explanation: The party was formed in Ripon to fight against slavery, so today's crop of Republicans would be horrified!

question: The first kindergarten in the US was established in this state. (State trivia question)
explanation: Margarethe Schurz started it in 1856, and taught only in German in a house in Watertown, and the town still celebrates Kinderfest each September.

question: You can find the House on the Rock, an unusual structure and collection of oddities, in this state. (State trivia question)
explanation: The structure was built starting in 1945 by Alex Jordan Jr. It is considered an oddity because it actually contains almost nothing related to rock, geology or music.

question: The first practical mechanical typewriter was invented in Milwaukee in this state in 1868 by Christopher Latham Sholes. (State trivia question)
explanation: Interestingly, this is the same person who came up with the QWERTY keyboard layout, but he may not have developed that layout to slow down typing, as is commonly believed.

question: This is the only state whose flag has an image of an animal on both sides
explanation: The state seal contains a woman and a cowboy, and an elk and a bison serve as state animals on the state flag.

question: This state boasts the first national monument (Devil's Tower) designated in the US, created in 1906 by Theodore Roosevelt
explanation: The monolith is about 867 ft from base to summit. It was also the site where a spaceship landed in the movie Close Encounters of the Third Kind.

question: The westernmost point that a Confederate soldier ever reached was in this state during the Civil War.
explanation: That soldier was Capt. John McMurty, who was killed by Native Americans in what is now Story, Wyo.

question: This state's license plates feature a bucking horse and rider
explanation: The image began appearing on license plates in 1936, and is now a registered trademark of the state. So you can't even copy a license plate from the state for use on your scooter!

question: This is the least populated state, and the only one with fewer than 600,000 people.
explanation: That's fewer people than live in most large cities. Or that subscribe to some Youtubers.

question: In this state, it is illegal to photograph rabbits from January to April, unless you have a special permit
explanation: It is thought that this law was passed to protect rabbit migration and breeding during those months, but it is actually an urban legend. There is no such law.

question: This is the only state that is almost a perfect rectangle
explanation: It has borders at 41 and 45 degrees north latitude and 104 and 111 degrees west longitude, but is technically a parellelogram, not a rectangle.
